How have Americans worked to make unfair rules fair for everyone?
slavery. When people are owned by other people and forced to work without pay. It was legal in parts of the U.S. until 1865.
freedom seeker. A person who escaped from slavery to be free. Harriet Tubman was a freedom seeker.
amendment. A change or addition to the U.S. Constitution. The 13th Amendment ended slavery.
civil rights. The rights every citizen should have, like voting and being treated fairly by the law.
boycott. When people stop buying or using something to protest an unfair rule. Example: the Montgomery Bus Boycott.
nonviolence. Working for change in peaceful ways, without hurting anyone.
union. A group of workers who join together to ask for fair pay and safe work.
Long ago, slavery was legal in parts of the United States. Enslaved people were forced to work without pay. Their families could be split apart. Many people worked hard to end this unfair system.

I ask: who ended slavery? Not just one person. Many enslaved people escaped as freedom seekers . People like Harriet Tubman helped them. Almost 200,000 Black soldiers and sailors fought for the North. President Lincoln signed an order. Then the 13th Amendment ended slavery in 1865.

Lincoln said slavery was wrong. But in 1862, he wrote a letter. He said his main goal was to save the Union , or keep the country together. Later, he decided that freeing enslaved people would help win the war. Then he pushed for the 13th Amendment. His ideas changed over time. Historians look at his own letters to know this.

Even after slavery ended, many unfair laws stayed. In the South, segregation laws kept Black and white people apart. In Montgomery, Alabama, Black riders had to give up bus seats to white riders. In 1955, people joined together to change this.

Let me compare two ways to change a rule. Way 1: fight and hurt people. Way 2: refuse to ride the bus, march and speak. Dr. King chose Way 2. This is called nonviolence . A boycott is a nonviolent tool. When riders stopped using buses, the bus company lost money. Then leaders had to listen.

Many books tell only about Rosa Parks and Dr. King. Who else made the boycott work? Thousands of Black riders walked to work for more than a year. Jo Ann Robinson and other women printed thousands of flyers overnight. And nine months before Rosa Parks, a girl named Claudette Colvin did the same. She was 15. She also refused to give up her seat. Change takes many people!

Farmworkers pick the fruits and vegetables we eat. In the 1960s, many in California earned very little. They worked long, hot days. Often they had no clean water or bathrooms. Many were Mexican American and Filipino American. They formed a union to ask for fair pay.

How can workers with little money get power? One worker alone can be ignored. But a union speaks for many. In 1965, Filipino American grape pickers, led by Larry Itliong, went on strike . The union Dolores Huerta helped lead joined them. They asked families across the country to stop buying grapes. Many did! In 1970, grape growers signed agreements for better pay.

In 1972, Dolores Huerta heard people say, "No, it can't be done." She answered, " Sí, se puede! " That is Spanish for "Yes, it can be done!" The words became a famous cheer. People still use it today. It means: together, we can make things fair.

Rosa Parks wrote that people often said she kept her seat because she was tired. She said that was not true. Then she wrote: I was not tired physically, or no more tired than I usually was at the end of a working day. I was not old, although some people have an image of me as being old then. I was forty-two. No, the only tired I was, was tired of giving in. Word help: physically means in my body. Giving in means going along with something unfair. Facts: Rosa Parks worked sewing clothes in a department store. She was also a leader in the Montgomery NAACP, a group that worked for civil rights.

Abraham Lincoln. The 16th President of the United States. He led the country during the Civil War. In 1863, he signed the Emancipation Proclamation . He pushed Congress to pass the 13th Amendment, which ended slavery. At first, his main goal was to keep the country together.

Harriet Tubman. She was born enslaved in Maryland. In 1849, she escaped to freedom. She went back about 13 times. She guided about 70 people to freedom on the Underground Railroad . It was a secret path of helpers and safe houses. In the Civil War, she was a scout and nurse. She helped free more than 700 people in one raid.

Rosa Parks. A civil rights leader in Montgomery, Alabama. On December 1, 1955, she would not give up her bus seat to a white rider. She was arrested. Her brave act helped start the Montgomery Bus Boycott. She kept working for fairness her whole life.

Martin Luther King Jr.. A pastor from Atlanta, Georgia. He led the bus boycott and taught nonviolence . In 1963, he gave his "I Have a Dream" speech to about 250,000 people. In 1964, he won the Nobel Peace Prize. He was killed in 1968. We honor him on Martin Luther King Jr. Day in January.

Dolores Huerta. A teacher who grew up in California. She saw her students come to school hungry. So she worked to help their farmworker families. In 1962, she and César Chávez started a union for farmworkers. It became the United Farm Workers. She made up the cheer " Sí, se puede! "

Larry Itliong. He came to the United States from the Philippines at age 15. He worked on farms for many years. In 1965, he led Filipino American grape pickers on strike in Delano, California. He asked the union Dolores Huerta helped lead to join. Together, they won better pay.
